the small intestine, where they are broken down by pancreatic

stimulated by the infant’s bile salts and hydrolyzes the triglycerides

ides, fatty acids, and lecithin, aid in the intestinal digestion of fat.
The activities of the enzymes responsible for the digestion of 
disaccharides—maltase, isomaltase, and sucrase—reach adult 
levels by 28 to 32 weeks’ gestation. Lactase activity (responsible 
for digesting the disaccharide in milk) reaches adult levels by 
birth. Pancreatic amylase, which digests starch, continues to 
remain low during the first 6 months after birth. If the infant 
consumes starch before this time, increased activity of salivary 
amylase and digestion in the colon usually compensate.
The neonate has functional but physiologically immature 
kidneys that increase in size and concentrating capacity in the 
early weeks of life. The kidneys double in weight by 6 months
